name: The Unmapped Hours
description:
A live recording from a single legendary performance by Thresh & The Undertow, captured on February 14th, 2204, at a relocated underground venue in the Circuit district known that night only as 'the Furnace Room' — its actual location was a decommissioned water treatment plant in Tier 2's industrial western corridor. The show was unannounced until six hours before doors, distributed via encrypted mesh invitation to fewer than 300 people. The recording was made by audience member Saoirse Adeyemi-Pryce on a modified analog tape rig, with secondary digital capture by three others in attendance. The resulting composite recording, assembled over four months, captures the full four-hour performance with only minor gaps.

Thresh & The Undertow performed their entire catalog that night alongside forty minutes of material never recorded in studio. Standout moments include an extended version of 'Corridor Ruin' that stretches to twenty-two minutes, incorporating live improvisation where lead vocalist Caius Ndlovu-Ferreira negotiates the melody with the crowd in real time — at several points the audience is singing harmonics back to the band, and the recording captures this as a single organism breathing. 'Saltline' — a previously unreleased track about the slow chemical contamination of Tier 1's water supply — was performed once that night and never again; Ndlovu-Ferreira has never explained why. The album closes with a cover of a pre-Meridian folk song, its origin debated by scholars, performed a cappella by the full band and a significant portion of the crowd.
creator: Thresh & The Undertow
audience: Tier 1 and Tier 2 music communities, underground circuit regulars, folk music historians, those who were present at the original show
cultural_impact: The Unmapped Hours occupies a specific and irreplaceable position in Meridian 88's underground music culture — it is simultaneously a document, a relic, and a myth. The 'Saltline' track has generated sustained speculation: water rights activists believe it contains coded information about the contamination's corporate origin that Thresh & The Undertow were legally pressured not to release in studio. Whether or not this is true, the track has been analyzed obsessively, and fragments of it appear in subsequent protest music. The recording itself, distributed in generations of copies each slightly degraded, has developed an almost liturgical status among Shelf and Circuit music communities.
known_fans: those who attended the original show
story_hooks: The original uncompressed master recordings from that night — Saoirse Adeyemi-Pryce's analog tapes — have surfaced in an estate auction. Multiple parties want them: a Vantablack archivist, a water rights legal team who believe 'Saltline' contains admissible evidence, and someone claiming to represent Caius Ndlovu-Ferreira personally.

A Tier 3 academic studying the album's provenance has traced the pre-Meridian folk song covered at the end to a specific community displaced during the city's original construction — and descendants of that community want recognition, or something more.

Thresh & The Undertow has quietly announced a reunion, their first performance in eleven years, and the location system — mesh-distributed invitations, six-hour notice — is active again. Someone is paying the players to find the venue before the show starts.
